title: Schweinshaxe
subtitle: Bavarian roasted pork knuckle
excerpt: Schweinshaxe is the showpiece of Bavarian cooking. The pork knuckle roasts low and slow until the meat is falling tender, then a blast of high heat turns the skin to crackling. It is bold, rich, and deeply satisfying.
sourceNotes: Schweinshaxe is a staple of Bavarian beer halls. It is served at Oktoberfest and bierkellers across Munich. The dish is known for its dramatically crisp crackling and tender meat.

recipe.temperatureNote: Start at 160°C for 2 hours, then raise to 220°C for 30 minutes to crisp the skin.

content.text: Schweinshaxe is Bavarian pub food at its finest. You need two things: scored skin and a two-stage oven. Low heat makes the meat tender. High heat makes the crackling. Do not skip either stage.

items.prepNote: cut into 2 large pieces with skin scored in a crosshatch

content.text: Score the pork skin in a crosshatch pattern with a sharp knife. Rub all over with crushed garlic, caraway seeds, and salt flakes. Get the rub into the scored cuts.
Place the onion halves cut-side down in a roasting tin. Sit the pork pieces on top of the onion. Pour the beer and stock around the pork -- not over the skin.
Roast at 160°C for 2 hours. The meat should be very tender and starting to pull away from the bone.
Remove the pork from the tin. Pat the skin completely dry with kitchen paper. Return to the tin on a rack if you have one, or directly in the tin.
Raise the oven to 220°C. Roast for 25-30 minutes until the skin is blistered and deeply golden. Watch closely in the final 10 minutes.
Rest for 10 minutes before serving. Serve with sauerkraut, potato dumplings, or mustard.

items.cause: Moisture on the skin before the final blast
items.fix: Pat the skin completely dry before raising the heat and remove from any liquid

content.text: Schweinshaxe is inseparable from Bavaria. It is the dish of Oktoberfest, served on wooden boards at long communal tables with litre mugs of beer. Munich's bierkellers -- Hofbraeuhaus and Augustiner among them -- have served it for well over a century. It also appears at Christmas markets across Germany.
